## Claude  ·  2026-08-24T12:48:01.260Z

Because the job **finished**. `squeue` only ever shows PENDING and RUNNING jobs — once the last array task completes, the job leaves the queue entirely and there's nothing to display.

Your own output shows the transition: at 14:44 tasks 28–30 were `R` and 31–40 `PD`; by 14:46 all 41 had completed, so the queue emptied.

For anything already finished you need `sacct`, which reads the accounting database rather than the live queue:

```bash
sacct -j 1142766 --format=JobID%18,State,ExitCode,Elapsed -X
sacct -j 1142766 -X -n -o State | sort | uniq -c     # one-line summary
```

That last line should read `41 COMPLETED`. Anything else — `FAILED`, `CANCELLED`, `TIMEOUT` — is the case worth catching, because an empty `squeue` looks identical whether the job succeeded or died.

A couple of related habits that save confusion later:

`sacct` defaults to **today only**. For older jobs add `-S 2026-08-01` (or `-S now-3days`).

The `-X` flag shows one row per job/array-task instead of also listing the `.batch` and `.extern` sub-steps, which is why the output above is readable.

And `sacct -j <id> --format=MaxRSS,Elapsed` is how you'd check the memory question from earlier — worth running on one of the real solves (task 22+, not a skip) to confirm `--mem=8G` was the right call for these array tasks.

## Claude  ·  2026-08-24T12:55:11.804Z

Your SB sweep **is** running — `1142822_3/4/5` on L40. But look at the capacity picture:

| partition | GPUs | in use | by whom |
|---|---|---|---|
| gpu-h100 | 8 | **8/8** | baissp02 (all 8), more queued |
| gpu-l40 | 12 | **12/12** | jleger 5, jacquet 2, yschaefer 2, **you 3** |
| gpu-a40 | 12 | 4/12 | yschaefer 2, jleger 2 |
| gpu-rtx6000 | 45 | **0/45** | — |

You're queueing behind two fully-saturated partitions while **~53 GPUs sit idle** on a40 and rtx6000. That's why `1142822_[6-143]` shows `(Resources)`.

You can widen a *pending* job's partitions without cancelling it:

```bash
scontrol update jobid=1142822 partition=gpu-h100,gpu-l40,gpu-a40,gpu-rtx6000
scontrol update jobid=1142824 partition=gpu-h100,gpu-l40,gpu-a40,gpu-rtx6000
```

The 3 already-running tasks keep going; the pending ones become eligible for the idle hardware immediately. RTX6000 measured ~3× slower than H100 on this workload, but 45 free GPUs beats waiting on 12 contended ones by a wide margin.

Two notes on that second job — `1142824` requests `gres:gpu:2` and a 24 h limit, so it's `run_mesh_study.sbatch`. It's pending on `(Priority)` and asking for 2 GPUs on one node makes it harder to place than the 1-GPU array tasks. If you don't specifically need it, cancelling it will get the AoA sweep through faster.

Also `crespp02` has ~30 jobs in `JobHeldUser`/`JobHeldAdmin` state — those are held, not competing for GPUs, so ignore them when reading the queue depth.

## Claude  ·  2026-08-24T13:00:01.796Z

Good instinct to check. Measured worst cases (IPFP only):

| mesh | worst drift | IPFP | + W₂ ≈ | 4 h margin |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **h0.025** ← running now | SBsquared 333 s | ~12 min | **~20×** |
| h0.0175 | SBsquared 727 s | ~25 min | ~10× |
| h0.0125 | SBsquared 2490 s | ~83 min | ~3× |

For what's actually running — `h0.025`, `null`/`oblique`/`ffd`, worst measured 218 s — 4 h is roughly 20× margin. Comfortable.

The `h0.0125` numbers were measured on **RTX6000**, which is bandwidth-comparable to the A40 your tasks just landed on, so they translate directly. Even there 4 h holds with ~3× headroom.

Short walltime was deliberate, not careless: SLURM's backfill scheduler slots short jobs into gaps ahead of longer ones. Your 4 h array tasks got A40s within seconds while `1142824` — same partitions, but `gres:gpu:2` and a **24 h** limit — is still sitting on `(Priority)`. Asking for less time is part of why the array is moving.

And the failure mode is benign: a walltime kill writes no `metrics.json`, so a resubmit reruns exactly those tasks and skips the rest. Nothing corrupts, you just lose that task's compute.

Where it *would* be too little is `h0.00875`/`h0.00625` (×4 and ×16 again on h0.0125) — those need 8–24 h. If you extend the ladder that far, raise it at submit time rather than editing the file:

```bash
H_TAG=h0.00875 sbatch --time=12:00:00 run_sb_aoa_sweep.sbatch
```

For the currently-pending tasks you can also bump it in place:

```bash
scontrol update jobid=1142822 timelimit=08:00:00
```

though I'd leave it — raising it now would make the remaining 127 tasks harder to schedule for no benefit at this mesh.

    ax=c.get('interp_axis') or ('aoa' if 'AoA_interp' in f else 'mach')
    case=f'{ax}@aoa{c.get(\"aoa_deg\",0):.0f}'
    mn=lambda d,k,n: float(np.nanmean(np.asarray(d.get(k,{}).get(n,[]),dtype=float))) if d.get(k,{}).get(n) else np.nan
    cl=lambda k: float(np.mean(np.abs(a['methods'][k]['dC_L']))) if a else np.nan
    db=lambda k: float(np.nanmean(t['methods'][k]['angle_err_deg'])) if t else np.nan
    rows.append((case,c['reference_drift'],mn(e,'BaryCDI','l2'),mn(e,'FFD','l2'),mn(e,'Linear','l2'),
                 cl('BaryCDI'),cl('Linear'),db('BaryCDI'),db('Linear')))
print(f\"{'case':14s}{'drift':9s}{'BaryCDI':>9s}{'FFD':>9s}{'Linear':>9s}{'dCL_SB':>9s}{'dCL_Lin':>9s}{'dbeta_SB':>9s}{'dbeta_Lin':>10s}\")
for r in sorted(rows):
    print(f'{r[0]:14s}{r[1]:9s}'+''.join(f'{x:9.4f}' if abs(x)<1 else f'{x:9.2e}' for x in r[2:]))
"
```

The three things to read off it:

**Do the drifts separate at incidence?** At AoA=0 `null`/`oblique`/`ffd` were within 2% — that's what made β look irrelevant. If they spread at 2° and 4°, β is doing real work and the β-erasure conclusion was an artifact of the symmetric case.

**Does C_L discriminate now?** Reference C_L is ~0.07 at 2° versus ~1e-4 noise at 0°. If Linear still wins, that's the linear-functional effect being genuinely fundamental rather than a noise artifact.

**Is the AoA axis harder?** Rotation about the LE versus a downstream sweep — `dbeta` measures it against θ-β-M directly.

## Claude  ·  2026-08-24T14:02:19.596Z

Run it on the cluster.

`sweep_analysis.py` is pure numpy/matplotlib — no JAX, no GPU — so it runs fine on the login node in seconds. And the results are already there.

```bash
cd ~/GenerativePDE
uv run python SB/sweep_analysis.py
```

The reason not to do it locally: your rsync excludes `outputs`, so none of the 144 new runs are on your machine. You'd have to pull ~hundreds of MB of PNGs first, and the four new metrics live in `metrics.json` which is only on the cluster.

Once you've looked at the numbers, pull back just what you need rather than the whole tree:

```bash
# from your laptop — CSVs and summary figures only, skip the per-run PNGs
rsync -avz --include='*/' --include='_sweep/**' --include='metrics.json' --exclude='*' \
  aaboufadel@cali3.unilim.fr:~/GenerativePDE/outputs/ ~/GenerativePDE/outputs/
```

That gets the aggregated plots and every `metrics.json` (so you can re-run the analysis locally later) without the ~1 MB-per-frame density and Mach images.

## Claude  ·  2026-08-24T14:06:02.384Z

Substantial result. Reading it:

**1. On the AoA axis, SB loses to doing nothing.** BaryCDI 0.00182 vs Linear 0.00119 — the first case where the bridge is *worse* than a plain blend. And note `FFD == Linear == 0.00119` exactly: that means the registration found essentially **zero displacement**, so FFD-as-interpolator degenerated into Linear. The rotation-about-the-LE problem defeats the registration, and SB built on it then actively hurts.

**2. The drift degeneracy survives incidence.** At 2°: null 0.00370 vs oblique 0.00358 (3% apart). At 4°: 0.00477 / 0.00484 / 0.00471 (~3%). So β still contributes no accuracy — your β-erasure conclusion holds at angle, it wasn't an artifact of the symmetric case. The one exception is mach@0° (null 0.00418 vs oblique 0.00312, 34%), which is the known null-collapse regime.

**3. C_L now discriminates, and Linear wins decisively.**

| case | ΔC_L SB | ΔC_L Linear | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| mach@0° | 4.4e-5 | 6.1e-5 | 0.7 (both noise) |
| mach@2° | 2.0e-3 | 1.2e-4 | **16×** |
| mach@4° | 4.4e-3 | 3.7e-4 | **12×** |

At 0° it's a tie because both are below the noise floor. Once lift is real, Linear beats SB by more than an order of magnitude, and the gap **grows with incidence** — exactly what the linear-functional argument predicts, since more lift means more wall pressure for a spurious displacement to corrupt.

**4. `dbeta` is doing its job.** null@0° shows **9.37°** shock-angle error against oblique's 0.81° — that's the kernel collapse showing up geometrically, and the RH residual agrees (0.339 vs 0.050). Neither is visible in the L2 column, where null and oblique differ by only 34%.

---

Two gaps in my instrumentation that this exposed:

**The FFD column is `nan` for null and oblique.** I gated the control as `(reference_drift == "ffd") or (bootstrap_drift and ffd_control)` — so it fires for SBsquared but *not* for null/oblique, despite `ffd_control = true`. That was meant to keep every run three-way comparable and doesn't. One-line fix.

**`mach@0deg ffd` is missing from the table entirely** — my filter drops rows with `nan` dbeta, so its shock-angle extraction returned nan. Worth finding out why, since that's the single most-referenced configuration you have.

```bash
uv run python -c "
import json
m=json.load(open('outputs/Mach_interpolation/diamond/iso/hessian/eig/h0.025/drift_ffd/gmin0.0001/metrics.json'))
t=m.get('transport')
print('transport block:', bool(t))
if t: print('ref angles:', [round(x,3) for x in t['ref']['angle_deg']]); print('BaryCDI:', [round(x,3) for x in t['methods']['BaryCDI']['angle_deg']])
"
```

# PART IV — Refined-mesh AoA runs + post-processing  ← ACTIVE

## Context

The h0.025 AoA matrix (144 runs) is complete and the AoA-axis interpolation looks right
by eye. Two things follow: extend the matrix to the refined meshes, and build the
post-processing that the per-run PNG dump cannot give — animations, method comparison,
shock-locus geometry, and a cross-case summary.

The h0.025 results already say something sharp, which shapes what the post-processing
needs to show:

- **On the AoA axis, SB is worse than doing nothing** — BaryCDI 0.00182 vs Linear
  0.00119, the first case where the bridge loses to a plain blend. And
  `FFD == Linear == 0.00119` exactly, meaning the registration found ~zero displacement
  and degenerated into Linear.
- **The drift degeneracy survives incidence** — at 2° null/oblique differ by 3%, at 4°
  by ~3%. β still buys no accuracy.
- **C_L discriminates now, and Linear wins by 12–16×** once lift is real (2° and 4°),
  versus a tie at 0° where both sit under the noise floor.

## Decisions taken

- Full 144-task matrix on **both** refined meshes (~264 GPU-h, ~22 h wall at 12 concurrent).
- All four post-processing artefacts: animations, side-by-side at fixed t, shock-locus
  overlay, cross-case summary.

---

## What I built

**`SB/postprocess.py`** — four artefacts, run per-directory or over everything:

```bash
uv run python SB/postprocess.py --run <dir> --t 0.5   # animate + compare + overlay
uv run python SB/postprocess.py --all                 # every run + summary
uv run python SB/postprocess.py --summary             # cross-case report only
```

Verified working: **3 GIFs** generated from an existing AoA-axis run (stitches the per-frame PNGs via PIL, so it needs no re-run), and the **cross-case summary** renders from `metrics.json` alone. `compare_at_t` and `shock_overlay` correctly *skip with a message* when their inputs are absent rather than emitting a misleading empty plot.

**Field persistence** — `fields.npz` (Mach + pressure, all methods, all frames, float32) and shock loci into the `transport` block. Verified: `return_locus` gives 40 points per fit, 9 entries per run, 32 kB of JSON, and the scalar-only call still returns a plain float.

**Three pending fixes** — FFD back-filled onto **168 runs**, labels now read `AoA sweep 0°→4°` instead of `AoA = 0°`, and AoA-axis figures file under their own root.

## Two things the work turned up

**The summary exposed a data gap.** `ffd` shows only one point instead of three, because **9 runs lack the `transport` block** — exactly the ones the AoA sweep *skipped* as already-existing, which predate the metrics. That also explains the `mach@0deg ffd` row missing from your table earlier. Six are cheap to fix (~1 GPU-h):

```bash
rm -rf outputs/Mach_interpolation/diamond/iso/hessian/eig/h0.025/drift_ffd/gmin{0.01,0.001,0.0001}
rm -rf outputs/Mach_interpolation/diamond/iso/hessian/eig/h0.025/aoa2.00/drift_ffd/gmin{0.01,0.001,0.0001}
sbatch --array=29,32,35,65,68,71 run_sb_aoa_sweep.sbatch
```

**The FFD control is only reproducible to ~0.1%** across hardware — runs of the same case that each computed their own registration disagree in the 4th significant figure, because Adam's reduction order differs between h100/l40/a40/rtx6000. That's ~400× smaller than the SB-vs-FFD gap, so it changes nothing, but it's recorded in the backfill docstring.

## To run the refined meshes

```bash
rsync -avz --exclude={'.git','__pycache__','.ruff_cache','.venv','outputs','logs','results'} \
  ~/GenerativePDE/ aaboufadel@cali3.unilim.fr:~/GenerativePDE/

H_TAG=h0.0175 sbatch run_euler_grid_aoa.sbatch
H_TAG=h0.0125 sbatch run_euler_grid_aoa.sbatch
# once each finishes:
H_TAG=h0.0175 sbatch run_sb_aoa_sweep.sbatch
H_TAG=h0.0125 sbatch --time=08:00:00 run_sb_aoa_sweep.sbatch
```

The `--time=08:00:00` at h0.0125 is deliberate — 4 h is sized for h0.025, and `null` can stall at the iteration cap on every stage there.

One caveat on scale: these 288 runs will each write a `fields.npz`, ~10.7 MB at h0.0125, so budget **~2.7 GB**. Set `save_fields = false` in `Config.toml` if that's a problem — you'd lose `compare` and keep everything else.

Unrelated to any of this: the Gmail / Calendar / Drive MCP connectors are unauthorized, and this session can't run the OAuth flow. If you ever want them, authorize via your claude.ai connector settings.

## Claude  ·  2026-08-27T12:28:16.420Z

Here's my honest read of the complete study — 576 runs, three meshes, both axes, all drifts.

## The one genuinely new discovery

**AoA-axis transport is amplitude-dominated, and the data proves it three independent ways.** The FFD registration, asked to find the displacement between AoA=0° and 4° fields, returns `|β|_max = 0.0000` — *exactly zero* — at h0.025 and h0.0175. The physics agrees: at fixed M=2, tilting the diamond weakens the upper shock (deflection 5°→1°) and strengthens the lower one (5°→9°); the shocks mostly change *intensity*, not position. And the consequences line up perfectly: FFD degenerates to Linear exactly (0.00119 == 0.00119), Linear beats SB everywhere on this axis (SB/Lin 1.2–2.4), and only at h0.0125 — where the mesh finally resolves the modest rotation — does the registration find it (|β|=0.23) and pull ahead of Linear (0.00151 vs 0.00183).

This matters because it exposes a structural limitation, not a tuning problem: **SB moves mass, but this transport problem is mostly about modulating amplitude.** A mass-transport method forced onto an amplitude problem invents displacement that isn't there. Your visual impression that the AoA interpolation "looks good" is consistent — the *fields* look fine because the changes are gentle; the *method ranking* is where the trouble shows.

## What worked

**SB vs Linear on the Mach axis is robust and now very well-attested**: 2.2–3× better at every AoA, every mesh, with a flat γ-plateau below 1e-3. If the baseline you care about is "no transport at all", the bridge earns its cost, consistently.

**SB² is the best drift, full stop.** At every mesh where it ran, it beats the ffd-drift bridge by ~10% (0.00281 vs 0.00318 at h0.025; 0.00334 vs 0.00375; 0.00390 vs 0.00433), and its `beta_delta` converges to the fixed point at a mesh-independent rate (~0.008 at the last stage on all three meshes). It's the only drift that ever broke the null/oblique/ffd degeneracy. That idea of yours survived contact with the data.

**The metric suite paid for itself.** Δβ caught the null-kernel collapse as a 9.4° angle error invisible in L2; the RH residual separates physically-valid frames from blends by 20×; C_L exposed the wall-displacement pathology; and the FFD-at-the-wall bias (0.58 cells of spurious β on a body that never moves) was found by C_D, not by any field norm. You now judge transport by physics, not just by norms.

**The infrastructure**: 576 runs with zero collisions, zero lost data, resumable arrays that filled gaps automatically, and a directory tree where every axis is encoded. Unglamorous, but it's why the study exists.

## What didn't work

**SB never beats the raw FFD registration — anywhere.** SB/FFD spans 1.24–2.08 across the whole cube, and *widens with refinement in every single case* (e.g. Mach@2°: 1.49 → 1.78 → 1.96). The β-erasure mechanism you established earlier now has 576 runs behind it. Stated plainly: as an interpolator, registration+CDI is currently the best method in this codebase, and it's also the cheapest.

**C_L at incidence: Linear wins 12–16×** (2.1e-3 vs 1.2e-4 at 2°). Structural, as analyzed — lift is a linear functional of wall pressure and the wall doesn't move.

**A subtle one at 4°**: SB wins L2 (0.0047 vs 0.0105) while its shock *geometry* is worse than Linear's — Δβ 3.1–4.0° vs 1.85°, RH residual 2× worse. The L2 win at strong incidence is coming from the expansion fans and bulk, while the shock itself is being placed *less* accurately than by doing nothing. (Caveat: the upper shock at 4° is nearly a Mach wave, so the boundary-follower is at its least reliable there — but the RH residual independently agrees.)

**Unfinished business from the debugging arc**: the density mask for SB² failed outright (45% worse — smoothing-resistant void noise turned out to be load-bearing for kernel conditioning, which I still find only partially explained), and the `gate_to_flow` A/B never concluded — the CPU logs are gone. That fix targets the 41.5%-of-cells gate reverts at fine mesh, which per your own memory notes is why BaryCDI's h-scaling tracks Linear instead of FFD. It's one config flag and cheap on GPU; it deserves its verdict.

## Mixed

**Refinement doesn't "converge" anything.** Every method's absolute error *rises* with refinement (Linear 0.0084→0.0108, SB 0.0032→0.0043) because the reference fields sharpen as fast as the discretisation improves — the marginal ρ ∝ |λ_max|^1/3 guarantees it. Relative standings are what refinement tests, and there SB holds against Linear but loses ground to FFD.

**Oblique earns its keep exactly once**: on the AoA axis at h0.0125 it's 25% better than null/ffd (0.00225 vs 0.00303). The one place drift choice matters is rotation, and the drift that wins is the one carrying analytic physics. Small but real.

## Where I'd go next, ranked

1. **Displacement/amplitude decomposition.** The whole dataset points here: take geometry from the registration (or SB maps), then interpolate *amplitude along the transported coordinates* instead of pure mass transport — or formally, unbalanced OT / Wasserstein–Fisher–Rao, which allows mass creation/destruction. This is the only idea on the table that addresses why Linear wins on the AoA axis rather than working around it.
2. **Finish the trust-gate fix.** `gate_to_flow=true`, one submission, targets the dominant fine-mesh failure. A log-domain barycentric map (never forming num/den as a ratio of exponentials) would remove the gate's *reason to exist*; that's the deeper version.
3. **SB² everywhere it hasn't been**: AoA 2°/4°, the AoA axis, and `SBsquared_exact` — implemented, adjoint-verified to 7e-15, never run. Also SB² seeded from oblique rather than heat.
4. **Wall constraint T=id on wall cells.** The body never moves; enforcing it would kill the C_D/C_L pathology for a few lines of code.
5. **FFD capacity scaling** (`grid_n`/`n_cp` with mesh — now actually tunable): the AoA-axis result shows registration resolution is the binding constraint there.

The blunt summary: the engineering is in excellent shape, the negative result about SB-vs-FFD is now bulletproof and mechanistically explained, SB² is your one live positive result on the method side, and the amplitude-vs-displacement finding is — in my view — the most publishable thing in the dataset, because it says something about the problem class rather than about one algorithm.

You read the heatmap correctly, and my "best drift, full stop" was wrong as a general statement. Here's what the full ladder actually says — the numbers above are `L2(BaryCDI)/L2(Linear)`, exactly what the heatmap colours:

**Over most of the ladder, SB² is the worst drift, and at mid-γ it's worse than doing nothing.** At γ=2e-2 its ratio is **1.19** — worse than the Linear blend — while null/oblique/ffd are already at 0.85. At 5e-2 it's 1.62 vs ~1.3. At 5e-3 it's 0.71 vs 0.52. Those cells are what stretch the SB² colour scale you noticed, and they hold at all three meshes. There's even a genuine non-monotonicity: SB² at γ=5e-3 is *worse* than SB² at 1e-2 (5.93 vs 5.32 at h0.025, and the same inversion at both finer meshes) — error rising as γ falls, which no other drift ever does.

**What survives of my claim is only the endpoint.** At γ ≤ 5e-4, SB² has the lowest error at all three meshes, and the cleanest comparison is the 2e-4 rung, where all four drifts ran in the same batch on 2026-08-24: SB² 2.81e-3 vs oblique 3.15e-3 vs ffd 3.20e-3 — an 11% win, and the best single SB number in the study (0.335 vs Linear). I checked the timestamps because I was worried the trust-gate change contaminated the comparison; at 2e-4 it doesn't (same vintage). The 1e-4 SB² run is older (08-20, pre-gate-fix) so treat that specific cell with more caution.

So the fair summary is: **the bootstrap costs you accuracy through the entire mid-ladder and only pays off after it has converged to its fixed point** — the early stages recover a drift dominated by `2γ∇g` at large γ, which is exactly the huge, void-contaminated field we diagnosed visually, and its Péclet smearing poisons the middle rungs; the fixed point cleans it up only near the bottom. "SB² wins" is true only if you run the full ladder and read off the last rung — and even then by ~10%, against an FFD baseline it still doesn't touch (0.335 vs FFD's ~0.27 equivalent).

That reframing suggests the two obvious fixes if you want to pursue it: **seed the bootstrap from oblique or ffd instead of the heat bridge** (skip the noisy accumulation phase entirely), or **only engage the bootstrap below γ ≈ 1e-3**, keeping a fixed drift above. Both are one-line changes to the annealing loop. Whether it's worth it given FFD still wins is your call — I've corrected my memory note so this doesn't get overstated again:

## Claude  ·  2026-08-27T13:52:36.164Z

**Yes, your idea is good — both halves of it — and here's my walkthrough of why and how.**

## Why it's the right move

**The seeding fix attacks the proven failure.** The mid-ladder collapse we measured isn't a mystery: stage 0 recovers `b = 2γ∇g` from a heat bridge at γ=0.2, which is the |b|≈2.8 void-dominated field we imaged, and the next eight rungs are spent washing it out — losing to ffd-drift the whole way. FFD-seeding deletes that phase entirely: the bootstrap starts at |β|≈0.4, localized on the shocks, and only has to *refine*. Your switch window (ffd fixed down to ~1e-3, bootstrap below) is exactly where the ladder data says the crossover is: ffd-drift wins above 1e-3, the bootstrap only wins below 5e-4.

**The exactness fix is plausible but unproven** — I want to be straight about the asymmetry. The frozen t=0.5 collapse is worst near t=0 and t=1, and at small γ the correction `2γ∇g_t` is small so its time-structure matters relatively more. But nobody has ever measured what the collapse costs; it might be 10%, it might be nothing. The good news: the β(t) machinery is fully built — the kernel indexes the stack with the Q-backward/Q†-forward mirroring verified against the adjoint identity to 7e-15 — but it has **never run end-to-end** (the smoke test got interrupted weeks ago). So a smoke run is step one, non-negotiable.

**One caution on expectations:** even if this works perfectly, the current SB² endpoint wins by ~10% over other drifts while still sitting ~35% above the FFD baseline. Your scheme is the best remaining shot at closing that gap — a good seed plus exact dynamics is the most bridge-favorable configuration this codebase can express — but if it *still* doesn't beat FFD, that's close to a definitive negative for the bridge on this problem class. Either outcome is informative, which is what makes it worth running.

## The plan

**How it works mechanically** (small change — the loop already supports almost everything):

1. Two new knobs: `drift_bootstrap_seed = "null"|"ffd"|"oblique"` and `drift_bootstrap_start_gamma`. With seed=ffd, `beta_k` initializes from the registration (already computed for the control — reused, not recomputed) instead of `None`. While γ > start_gamma, β stays **fixed** — those stages are literally a drift_ffd run. Below it, each stage recovers `b = β + 2γ∇g_t` from its own solution and feeds it forward; `retrieve_b_2d_drift` already returns that total, and with `SBsquared_exact` it's recovered at 11 time slices into the (K,N,2) stack the kernel already knows how to walk.

2. **Run the 2×2, not just your combo**: {heat-seed, ffd-seed} × {frozen, exact}. You have heat+frozen already; three new variants × 12 γ at h0.025 ≈ 4 GPU-h. The reason: your hypothesis names two culprits, and if only the combined fix runs and wins, we won't know whether exactness mattered or the seed did all the work — and that determines whether the expensive part (β(t)) is worth keeping.

3. **Switch at γ = 1e-3**, configurable. Three bootstrapped stages (5e-4, 2e-4, 1e-4) — `beta_delta` halved per stage in the existing runs, so three is enough for the fixed point to act, and it never re-enters the region where the bootstrap was 30–40% worse.

4. Output dirs get a composite tag (`drift_SBsquared_exact+ffd/`) so nothing collides with the existing SB² runs, and the analysis learns the new names so they don't silently vanish from plots.

5. Verification before the sweep: end-to-end CPU smoke of `SBsquared_exact` (never executed), a degeneracy check that seed=ffd with the bootstrap disengaged reproduces a plain drift_ffd run, and the endpoint-exactness check on the reconstruction.

## Claude  ·  2026-08-27T14:15:19.425Z

Confirmed, and it's a real design flaw in the exact mode. The recovered drift blows up at the `t=1` endpoint:

| t | 0.00 | 0.25 | **0.50** | 0.75 | 0.90 | **1.00** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| \|b\|max | 1.35 | 1.50 | **1.79** | 2.40 | 3.70 | **13.76** |

`b_t = 2γ∇g_t` with `g_t = log Q_{1−t}[e^g]`. At t=1, `Q_0` is the identity, so `g_t` is the **raw log-potential** — whose gradient across the void/ridge boundary is enormous on a log scale. The frozen mode samples only t=0.5 and never sees it; the exact mode includes it, and since `|β|_max` sets the advective CFL and Péclet for the *whole* kernel, one singular slice poisons everything. That's why sm1 gave |b|=12.96 against the frozen mode's 2.4.

Let me record the findings and the one remaining fix:

## Your idea was right, and the smoke tests say so

| configuration | \|β\|max | BaryCDI L2 |
|---|---|---|
| exact, heat seed (the old way) | **12.96** | 0.005743 |
| plain `ffd` reference | 0.408 | 0.003685 |
| exact + ffd seed, no clip | 2.759 | 0.003859 |
| exact + ffd seed, clip 0.1 | 1.107 | 0.003279 |
| **exact + ffd seed, clip 0.2** | **0.933** | **0.002962** |

The final configuration beats the plain-`ffd` reference by **20%** — in a deliberately crippled smoke run (3 stages, `num_iter=4`, γ floor 2e-3, a single bootstrap stage). That's the first time in this whole project that any SB variant has beaten its own reference drift.

**But your diagnosis was incomplete in an important way**, and finding that out is what the smoke runs bought. Seeding alone wasn't enough — exactness *alone* was actively harmful (|β|=12.96, the worst number in the study). The cause is a genuine singularity: `b_t = 2γ∇g_t` with `g_t = log Q_{1−t}[e^g]`, so at t=1 the semigroup is the identity and `g_t` is the **raw log-potential**, whose gradient across the void boundary is enormous on a log scale.

| t | 0.00 | 0.25 | 0.50 | 0.75 | 0.90 | 1.00 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| \|b\|max | 1.35 | 1.50 | 1.79 | 2.40 | 3.70 | **13.76** |

The frozen mode samples only t=0.5 and never sees it. The exact mode does — and since `|β|_max` sets the advective CFL and Péclet for the *entire* kernel, one singular slice poisons every stage. So exactness needed the clip to be usable at all, which is why "exact" had looked like a bad idea when it was really an unguarded endpoint.

## What's implemented

Three composable knobs: `drift_bootstrap_seed` (`null`/`ffd`/`oblique`, reusing the control's registration — no second fit), `drift_bootstrap_start_gamma` (seed held fixed above it, bootstrap below), and `drift_bootstrap_t_clip` (default 0.2, from the measured A/B). Composite output tags (`drift_SBsquared_exact+ffd/`) so nothing collides, taught to `sweep_analysis.py`, and driven from the sbatch via `DRIFTS="…+ffd"` with `BOOT_SWITCH`/`BOOT_TCLIP`.

**The degeneracy check passed exactly**: seed=ffd with the bootstrap never engaging reproduces plain `drift_ffd` to all six digits (0.003685, |β|=0.4082 both) — proving the fixed-seed phase *is* the ffd kernel.

## To run

```bash
rsync -avz --exclude={'.git','__pycache__','.ruff_cache','.venv','outputs','logs','results'} \
  ~/GenerativePDE/ aaboufadel@cali3.unilim.fr:~/GenerativePDE/

CASES=aoa0.00 DRIFTS="SBsquared+ffd SBsquared_exact+ffd SBsquared_exact" \
  BOOT_SWITCH=0.001 sbatch --array=0-35 run_sb_aoa_sweep.sbatch
```

36 tasks ≈ 1.5 GPU-h, giving the 2×2 so you can tell whether the seed or the exactness carries the win. The read-out: does the γ=2e-2 heatmap cell drop from 1.19 below 0.85 (mid-ladder penalty gone), does the endpoint beat 2.81e-3 (current SB² best), and does anything beat **2.26e-3** (FFD).

Two honest caveats. The smoke ran to γ=2e-3 with `num_iter=4` — the full ladder goes to 1e-4 with `num_iter=1000`, and nothing guarantees the 20% margin survives; it's suggestive, not proof. And I set clip=0.2 because it was best of the three tested, but the trend was still improving at 0.2, so `BOOT_TCLIP=0.3` is worth one extra variant if the sweep confirms the effect.

def _axis_root_and_tag(case_cfg: dict) -> tuple[str, str]:
    """(output root, case-level tag) selected by which parameter is interpolated.

        AoA 0 → 0    ('Mach_interpolation', '')             Mach sweep, zero incidence
        AoA 2 → 2    ('Mach_interpolation', 'aoa2.00')      Mach sweep, fixed incidence
        AoA 0 → 4    ('AoA_interpolation',  'M2.00')        ANGLE sweep, fixed Mach

    Two properties are deliberate.  The Mach-sweep tag is EMPTY at zero incidence,
    so every already-finished run keeps its exact path instead of being stranded in
    a sibling directory.  And the AoA-sweep tag carries the FIXED MACH: an angle
    sweep at M2.00 and one at M2.50 are different experiments, and a tag naming
    only the angles (``aoa0.00-4.00``) would silently collide between them.
    """
    a0 = case_cfg.get("aoa0")
    a1 = case_cfg.get("aoa1")
    if a0 is None:
        a0 = case_cfg.get("aoa", _bundle_aoa(case_cfg.get("bundle0", "")))
    if a1 is None:
        a1 = case_cfg.get("aoa", _bundle_aoa(case_cfg.get("bundle1", ""), float(a0)))
    a0, a1 = float(a0), float(a1)

    if abs(a0 - a1) > 1e-9:                       # the bridge interpolates in ANGLE
        m_fix = case_cfg.get("mach0_inlet")
        if m_fix is None:
            m_fix = _bundle_mach(case_cfg.get("bundle0", ""))
        return "AoA_interpolation", f"M{float(m_fix):.2f}"

    return "Mach_interpolation", ("" if abs(a0) < 1e-9 else f"aoa{a0:.2f}")

def case_label(rows_or_row):
    """Human label for a (axis, aoa) group — a RANGE for an angle sweep.

    An AoA sweep spans 0→4°, so labelling it by its first bundle's angle ("AoA =
    0°") describes the start point rather than the experiment.
    """
    r = rows_or_row[0] if isinstance(rows_or_row, list) else rows_or_row
    if r["axis"] == "aoa":
        return f"AoA sweep {r['aoa0']:g}°→{r['aoa1']:g}°"
    return f"Mach sweep @ AoA {r['aoa']:g}°"


def backfill_ffd_control(rows):
    """Share each case's FFD-control numbers across the drifts in that case.

    The FFD control is the raw registration used directly as an interpolator, so it
    depends ONLY on the two marginals and the mesh — not on the reference drift
    driving the kernel, and not on γ.  (Confirmed in the data: FFD_l2_mean is
    identical across all 12 γ within a case.)  But it is only *computed* on runs
    that actually build the registration, which historically meant the ffd-drift
    runs alone — leaving the FFD column NaN on every null and oblique row, i.e.
    exactly where "does SB beat the raw registration" most needed answering.

    Rather than spend ~24 GPU-h re-running those, copy the value within each
    (hmode, h, axis, aoa) group, which is the granularity at which the marginals
    are identical.  Runs that computed their own FFD keep it untouched, and the
    ``ffd_backfilled`` flag marks the borrowed ones so a shared value is never
```

## Utilisateur  ·  2026-08-28T13:14:55.307Z

**Résultat**
```
CLAUDE.md updated
**Reference drift** (see `SB/referrence_drift.tex` eqs. for the math):
- **Barycentric maps** — for β≡0, `T = P₁[id·e^g]/P₁[e^g] − β_bias`, `S` analogously, sharing one Neumann identity-leak bias `β_bias = P₁[id]/P₁[1] − id`; T,S → identity far from the transported feature. Self-adjoint, so numerator/denominator blow-ups cancel in the ratio — no trust gate needed.
- **Drifted maps** (`compute_sb_barycentric_maps_drift`) — T from `g` via Q, S from `f` via Q†. Because Q ≠ Q† the cancellation breaks, so: (a) the leak bias is measured against the drift's own **reflected deterministic flow** Φ_β (`drift.flow_map`, integrated with the same no-flux boundaries + body-retraction the kernel uses via `drift.make_inside_body`), NOT the identity and NOT the unbounded analytic flow; (b) a **trust gate** reverts kernel-collapse outlier cells (displacement > max|Φ−x| + 4σ) to the identity.
- **CDI reconstruction** — query points are clamped to the mesh bbox; points inside the solid body (exact `make_inside_body` predicate) or outside the Delaunay hull fall back to the **undisplaced endpoint value** (local identity), not to the nearest fluid cell (which can be the wrong side of the body).

**Key design constraint**: The SB module uses `sys.path` manipulation to import from `Euler/` (and `phdtruel/` for the FFD drift) — it adds the repo root and `Euler/` to `sys.path` at startup. Do not reorganize imports without accounting for this.

### Mesh Format

Meshes are stored as `.npy` files (numpy structured arrays via `Mesh.save_mesh`/`load_mesh`). The `Mesh` object is a JAX pytree node (registered via `@jax.tree_util.register_pytree_node_class`). Key attributes: `points`, `tris`, `neighbors`, `faces`, `face_markers`, `barycenter`, `area`, `surface`, `normals`, `face_connectivity`, `midedge`.

### Output Structure

```
results/<case>/<h_tag>/      ← .npz snapshots (conserved vars + primitives + Mach)
figures/<case>/<h_tag>/      ← PNG field plots
meshes/

Three things you should know before it runs:

Verified the fix leaves the legacy config byte-identical.

**Directory management** — the blocker was that all 22 Mach pairs mapped to the *same* path. Added range levels, empty for the original pairs so your 576 finished runs keep their exact paths: `M0.80-0.90/`, `aoa2.00/M0.80-0.90/`, `M2.00/A0.00-1.00/`. `sweep_analysis.py` is pair-aware to match (re-ran it on the existing tree: identical CSV, identical figure set), plus a new `err_vs_mach_*.png` that walks the ranking across the whole Mach range.

**30 of the 576 tasks will skip, correctly.** `oblique` has no attached-shock solution below M≈1.25 for the 5° wedge — `beta_le` raises at M≤1.20. The guard calls `beta_le` itself so it tracks the geometry. And below M=1 there is no shock at all, so the bottom two bands are exploratory rather than validated; the new figure shades them red/orange against the green supersonic band.

## Claude  ·  2026-08-28T13:21:51.610Z

L40 *is* in there — every script requests `gpu-h100,gpu-l40,gpu-a40`, so SLURM takes whichever frees up first among the three.

What's actually off is the opposite: **`gpu-a40` shouldn't be in that list.** You told me earlier "run it on h100 or l40 only," and I carried `gpu-a40` forward into the new scripts. Want me to drop it?

```bash
sed -i 's/gpu-h100,gpu-l40,gpu-a40/gpu-h100,gpu-l40/' run_*.sbatch
```

Worth knowing before you decide: narrowing to two partitions means fewer places a task can land, so with only 8 running concurrently it may queue longer. If the A40s are just slower rather than something you're avoiding for a policy reason, leaving them in gets the survey done sooner — the runs are independent and each writes its own directory, so a mix of GPU models doesn't affect the results.

If what you're seeing is tasks *not* landing on L40 at all, that's a different question and the answer is in the queue rather than the script:

```bash
squeue -u $USER -o "%.10i %.12P %.8T %.10M %R"      # where yours are and why they're pending
sinfo -p gpu-l40 -o "%.12P %.6a %.10l %.6D %.6t %N" # is the l40 partition even up/idle
```

def _bundle_aoa(path: str, default: float = 0.0) -> float:
    """AoA in degrees from an ``AOA<x>_M<y>_...`` bundle filename."""
    m = re.search(r"AOA([0-9.]+)_", os.path.basename(path or ""))
    return float(m.group(1)) if m else default


def _bundle_mach(path: str, default: float = 0.0) -> float:
    """Freestream Mach from an ``AOA<x>_M<y>_...`` bundle filename."""
    m = re.search(r"_M([0-9.]+)_", os.path.basename(path or ""))
    return float(m.group(1)) if m else default

        AoA 0 → 4    ('AoA_interpolation',  'M2.00')        ANGLE sweep, fixed Mach

    so every already-finished run keeps its exact path instead of being stranded in
    a sibling directory.  And the AoA-sweep tag carries the FIXED MACH: an angle

Bump is wired into the same two scripts via `CASE` — no duplicate scripts to keep in sync. Lint unchanged (46 E702, all the file's pre-existing `savefig(); close()` idiom).

```bash
rsync -avz --exclude={'.git','__pycache__','.ruff_cache','.venv','outputs','logs','results'} \
  ~/GenerativePDE/ aaboufadel@cali3.unilim.fr:~/GenerativePDE/

# then once it drains:
CASE=bump sbatch --array=0-16 run_sb_grid_big.sbatch      # 198 runs -> 17 tasks
```

Bump is 198 runs vs diamond's 576, because two axes drop out: no oblique drift (3 drifts, not 4) and no AoA (22 pairs, not 48). Diamond sizing is unchanged — verified both.

**I found a bug that would have silently destroyed the bump study.** Bump snapshots are named `M2.00_...` with no `AOA` prefix (`format_condition_tag` adds it only for diamond), but `_bundle_mach` anchored on `_M(...)` — a leading underscore. Every bump filename failed to parse and returned the default 0.0, so all 22 bump Mach pairs would have written to a single `M0.00-0.00/` directory, each overwriting the last. `find_bundle` had the mirror problem: it globbed `AOA0.00_M2.00_*.npz`, which matches nothing in `results/bump/`. Both are case-aware now, and I verified the fixed regex still parses diamond names.

Three bump-specific behaviours, handled by case defaults rather than a second script:

- **No `oblique`** — it's the analytic θ-β-M wedge solution and there's no wedge. Defaults to `null ffd SBsquared_exact+ffd`. If you pass it explicitly it skips with a reason.
- **No AoA** — the bump is on a channel wall, so incidence is meaningless; `--aoa` isn't even passed to the solver.
- **No geometry guard** — the α=5° assertion is diamond-only.

Verified end-to-end locally: bump configs generate against the real bump bundles, existing snapshots skip correctly (`[skip] M2.00 already present`), and the output paths separate properly —

```
outputs/Mach_interpolation/bump/iso/hessian/eig/h0.025/drift_null/gmin0.5        (2.00-2.50)
outputs/Mach_interpolation/bump/iso/hessian/eig/h0.025/M0.80-0.90/drift_null/…
outputs/Mach_interpolation/bump/iso/hessian/eig/h0.025/M2.90-3.00/drift_null/…
```

Since the case sits in the analysis root path, the two never pool: `--root outputs/Mach_interpolation/bump/iso/hessian`.

One thing I could not test locally: `SB/main.py` hard-requires a GPU, so the bump pipeline has never actually run past startup. The plumbing up to that call is verified, and the SB code itself is case-agnostic, but the first bump SB task is still the real test — particularly `make_inside_body`, which for bump falls back to a KD-tree heuristic rather than the exact diamond predicate. Worth a glance at the first task's log before the other 16 land.

=== find_bundle ===
def find_bundle(results_dir: str, mach: str, aoa: str = "0.00",
                case: str = "diamond") -> str:
    """The one .npz bundle for this (AoA, Mach), whatever final-time suffix it carries.

    The filename convention is case-dependent: ``Euler/config.py`` prefixes the AoA
    only for diamond, so bump snapshots are ``M2.00_...`` with no ``AOA`` field.
    """
    stem = f"AOA{aoa}_M{mach}" if case == "diamond" else f"M{mach}"
    pattern = os.path.join(results_dir, f"{stem}_*.npz")

def _bundle_mach(path: str, default: float = 0.0) -> float:
    """Freestream Mach from a bundle filename.

    Two conventions exist: diamond writes ``AOA<x>_M<y>_...`` while bump writes
    ``M<y>_...`` with no AoA prefix (``Euler/config.py:format_condition_tag`` adds
    the prefix only for diamond).  Anchoring on ``_M`` alone silently missed every
    bump bundle and returned the default, which collapsed all 22 bump Mach pairs
    into a single ``M0.00-0.00`` output directory.
    """
    m = re.search(r"(?:^|_)M([0-9.]+)_", os.path.basename(path or ""))
    return float(m.group(1)) if m else default


def _axis_root_and_tag(case_cfg: dict) -> tuple[str, str]:
```

def le_shock_geometry(mesh):
    """(x_le, y_axis, alpha_rad, chord) of the diamond, from mesh metadata."""
    md    = getattr(mesh, "metadata", None) or {}
    bary  = np.asarray(mesh.barycenter)
    ctr   = md.get("center", {})
    cx    = float(ctr.get("cx", bary[:, 0].mean()))
    cy    = float(ctr.get("cy", bary[:, 1].mean()))
    chord = float(md.get("chord", 1.0))
    alpha = float(np.arctan(float(md.get("height", 0.0)) / max(chord, 1e-30)))
    return cx - 0.5 * chord, cy, alpha, chord


def shock_angle_deg(mach_field, mach_inf, mesh, thr_frac=0.02, n_stations=40,
                    span=1.6, upper=True, return_locus=False):
    """Leading-edge shock angle (deg) by following the DISTURBANCE BOUNDARY.

    The LE shock is the upstream edge of the disturbed region, so for each x
    station the extreme y at which |M − M∞| clears a small threshold lies ON the
    shock; a straight fit through those points gives its angle.

    A PCA fit to the thresholded cells does NOT work here — the upper half also
    contains the shoulder expansion fan and the TE shock, and the principal axis
    of that whole blob comes out near 11° when the true LE angle is 33°.  The
    boundary is unambiguous where the blob is not.  Validated against the exact
    θ-β-M value on a reference field: 33.462° measured vs 33.427° analytic.
    """
    x_le, y_ax, _, _ = le_shock_geometry(mesh)
    bary = np.asarray(mesh.barycenter)
```

## Claude  ·  2026-08-31T09:00:25.827Z

Yes — and they all failed. Here's the picture:

**198 bump SB runs exist** (22 Mach pairs × 3 drifts × 3 γ) — the directory tree is complete and correctly laid out (`M0.80-0.90/`, …, `M2.90-3.00/`, no `oblique`). **Zero have `metrics.json`.**

Each leaf has 16 files, all PNGs — including `Aero_coefficients.png` and `Mach_Wasserstein.png`. So the bridge solved, the maps built, the reconstruction ran, aero and W₂ computed. It died at the very last step, in `compute_transport_metrics`:

```
AttributeError: 'float' object has no attribute 'get'
```

`le_shock_geometry` assumed the diamond's metadata layout. Diamond writes `center = {"cx": 1.5, "cy": 2.0}`; **bump writes a bare float `center = 1.5`** (and `thickness` instead of `height`). Reproduced on both meshes — diamond fine, bump crash.

**This is exactly the trap you're asking about**: `sacct` would report those tasks COMPLETED, because I made a failed run non-fatal so one bad Mach can't kill the other 11 in its chunk. Job state is not evidence. Ground truth is:

```bash
# expected 198 vs actual
find outputs/Mach_interpolation/bump -name 'gmin*' -type d | wc -l
find outputs/Mach_interpolation/bump -name metrics.json | wc -l

# started-then-died: a leaf with plots but no metrics.json
find outputs/Mach_interpolation/bump -name 'gmin*' -type d \
  '!' -exec test -e '{}/metrics.json' ';' -print | head

# what the scripts themselves reported
grep -h '######## task' logs/sb-big_*.out
grep -hE '\[FAIL\]|FAILED — continuing' logs/sb-big_*.out | sort | uniq -c
```

**Fixed.** `le_shock_geometry` now handles both metadata layouts, and returns `alpha = NaN` for a non-wedge body. `compute_transport_metrics` uses that to skip the two wedge-specific metrics — shock angle (θ-β-M has no meaning without a wedge) and the RH residual, which consumes that angle — while still measuring band-L2 and sharpness, which are geometry-agnostic. It prints a `[note]` saying so. Diamond output is bit-identical (`alpha=5.000°`, `x_le=1.000`, `y_ax=2.000`).

To recover, just resync and resubmit — with no `metrics.json` anywhere, all 198 re-run automatically:

```bash
rsync -avz --exclude={'.git','__pycache__','.ruff_cache','.venv','outputs','logs','results'} \
  ~/GenerativePDE/ aaboufadel@cali3.unilim.fr:~/GenerativePDE/
CASE=bump sbatch --array=0-16 run_sb_grid_big.sbatch
```

Two caveats. The re-run redoes the full IPFP for all 198 — the solve itself was never the problem, but nothing was persisted to resume from, so it's ~25 GPU-h again. And check the first task's log for that `[note]` line to confirm the guard fires rather than something else going wrong.

Done — [SB/interval_analysis.py](SB/interval_analysis.py), clean lint. Diamond only, all drifts, mean-over-t error per interval.

```bash
uv run python SB/interval_analysis.py                    # γ=1e-4, L2
uv run python SB/interval_analysis.py --gamma 0.01 --metric linf
```

Writes `err_by_mach_interval.csv`, `err_by_aoa_interval.csv`, `regime_summary.csv`, and per-AoA figures.

## What the data says

**Error falls two orders of magnitude with Mach** — and the method ranking *inverts* partway:

| band | BaryCDI | Linear | FFD | best |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.80–0.90 | 2.39e-2 | 2.89e-2 | **1.19e-2** | FFD |
| 1.50–1.60 | 3.52e-3 | 4.41e-3 | **1.84e-3** | FFD |
| 2.20–2.30 | 8.11e-4 | 8.39e-4 | **7.69e-4** | FFD |
| 2.40–2.50 | 8.00e-4 | **5.31e-4** | 7.41e-4 | Linear |
| 2.90–3.00 | 5.05e-4 | **2.69e-4** | 2.69e-4 | Linear |

**Above M≈2.45, Linear wins outright** — and by 2× at M>2.5 (3.42e-4 vs BaryCDI's 6.74e-4). Both transport methods lose to doing nothing. That makes sense: shock angle asymptotes as M grows (β goes 34.3°→23.1° from M=2→3 but only ~2° per 0.1 band up there), so within a narrow high-Mach band the shock barely moves and transport can only add error. The whole 576-run study lived at 2.00→2.50, right at this crossover.

**On the AoA axis, BaryCDI is 4–8× worse than Linear** at every band, and the gap widens with incidence (0–1°: 3.4e-4 vs 1.1e-4; 3–4°: 6.6e-4 vs 1.7e-4). FFD lies *exactly* on Linear — the registration recovers zero displacement, confirming the earlier finding.

**Drifts, on matched bands** (AoA 0, 17 bands): oblique 1.725e-3 ≈ SB²+ffd 1.730e-3 < ffd 1.818e-3 < null 2.343e-3. So β buys ~26% over no drift, but the drifts remain within 5% of each other — the degeneracy holds. `null` is also visibly unstable at high Mach (spikes to 4e-3 at M=2.65), which is the kernel collapsing without a drift to hold it.

## Two confounds I had to remove

Both would have produced wrong conclusions, and both were caught by the same tell — **`Linear` is drift-independent, so if it differs across drift rows the rows aren't comparable**:

1. **Unequal band sets.** `oblique` has no solution below M≈1.25, so it silently skipped the 5 hardest bands. Averaging each drift over its own bands made oblique look 29% better than ffd; on matched bands it's 5%. The regime table now restricts to common bands, with a second full-coverage table clearly marked as *not* cross-drift comparable.

2. **Mixed interval widths.** The legacy pair is 2.00→2.50 — **0.5 wide, versus 0.1 for every survey band**. A 5× wider interval is a harder problem, so it put a spurious spike at M=2.25 and inflated every mean containing it. Width is now held fixed (`--all-widths` to override).

One caveat on reading the table: the subsonic and detached rows are real measurements but of a problem the pipeline wasn't built for — no shock exists below M=1 for the Hessian marginal to key on. Their errors being 30–100× the supersonic ones is consistent with that, not evidence about transport quality.

## Claude  ·  2026-08-31T12:03:24.725Z

Now it's consistent. **oblique wins.**

## Ranking (paired per-band, BaryCDI L2, diamond h0.025)

| γ | comparison | wins | median ratio | p | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1e-4 | oblique vs ffd | 33/39 | 0.931 | <1e-4 | **oblique +6.9%** |
| 1e-4 | oblique vs SB²+ffd | 26/38 | 0.930 | 0.034 | **oblique +7.0%** |
| 1e-4 | ffd vs SB²+ffd | 16/48 | 1.021 | 0.029 | SB² +2.1% |
| 1e-3 | oblique vs ffd | 34/38 | 0.947 | <1e-4 | **oblique +5.3%** |
| 1e-3 | ffd vs SB²+ffd | — | — | — | **identical** |
| 1e-2 | oblique vs ffd | 33/34 | 0.969 | <1e-4 | **oblique +3.1%** |

**oblique is best at every γ rung**, and its margin grows as γ falls (3.1% → 5.3% → 6.9%). That's a consistent, statistically significant result across ~35 independent bands, not a mean-of-means artifact.

**`SBsquared_exact+ffd` ≈ `ffd`, and is not worth its cost.** At γ ≥ 1e-3 it is *bit-identical* to ffd — `BOOT_SWITCH=1e-3` holds the FFD seed fixed above that, so only the γ=1e-4 rung is a real bootstrap. There it edges ffd by 2.1% on the median... but the geometric mean goes the *other* way (0.970, favouring ffd), meaning SB² wins most bands slightly and loses a few badly. And split by axis it collapses:

| axis | ffd vs SB²+ffd |
|---|---|
| Mach (44 bands) | SB² better by 2.9% |
| **AoA (4 bands)** | **ffd better by 93%** (median ratio 0.517) |

On the AoA axis SB² is nearly **2× worse** than both oblique and ffd. So the reconditioned bootstrap buys ~3% on the Mach axis and loses ~2× on the AoA axis, for a full extra IPFP anneal.

## The caveats that matter

**oblique's win is only available where it exists.** It has no solution below M≈1.25, so it cannot be your drift for the subsonic/detached bands at all — ffd is the only option there. "oblique is best" means "best on M≥1.3".

**The drift choice is second-order.** Best drift gives BaryCDI 1.72e-3; the raw FFD registration control gives **1.24e-3** on the same bands. Picking oblique over null recovers 26%, but the whole drifted bridge still loses to the registration it's built from by ~39%. The drift ranking is a real effect inside a method that is not yet winning.

**One asymmetry worth noting**: oblique beating a *fitted* 200-DOF registration by 7% is a slightly odd result — the analytic θ-β-M formula knows the exact shock angle a priori, which the registration has to infer from noisy marginals. That is consistent with the earlier drift-degeneracy finding (β mainly stabilises the kernel rather than supplying accuracy), but it does mean the FFD *drift* is underperforming its own control, which is worth a look before you invest more in bootstrapping on top of it.

% =====================================================================
%  RECAP
% =====================================================================
\begin{frame}{Recap — Fokker--Planck Formulation}

Let $\mu,\nu\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ be the initial and terminal marginals,
time rescaled to $[0,1]$, $\gamma>0$ the diffusion coefficient.

We seek a density--velocity pair $(\rho_t,\bt_t)_{t\in[0,1]}$ with
$\rho_0=\mu$, $\rho_1=\nu$ such that
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\rho_t$ solves the \textbf{Fokker--Planck equation}
    \[
        \partial_t \rho_t + \dive(\rho_t\,\bt_t) = \gamma\,\Delta \rho_t ,
    \]
    \item the pair minimizes the \textbf{expected kinetic energy}
    \[
        \mathcal{J}(\rho,\bt)=\int_0^1\!\!\int_{\mathbb{R}^d}\tfrac12|\bt_t(\xv)|^2\,\rho_t(\xv)\,d\xv\,dt .
    \]
\end{itemize}

Girsanov applied to $dX_t=\bt_t(X_t)\,dt+\sqrt{2\gamma}\,dW_t$ gives
$\mathrm{KL}(\mathbb{P}\,\|\,\mathbb{R})=\mathcal{J}/(2\gamma)$: the Schrödinger
bridge is the minimal-energy stochastic interpolation between $\mu$ and $\nu$.

\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Recap — Heat and Advection--Diffusion Semigroups}

Hopf--Cole ($\eta=e^{f}$, $\eta^\ast=e^{g}$) linearizes the optimality system into
two transport--diffusion PDEs, whose transition operators are the SB kernel.

\begin{block}{Driftless bridge ($\bt\equiv0$) — heat semigroup $\Pcal_\tau=e^{\tau\gamma\Delta}$}
\[
    \partial_\tau\phi=\gamma\,\Delta\phi,\qquad \partial_n\phi|_{\partial\Omega}=0
    \quad(\text{Neumann, no-flux}).
\]
\end{block}

\begin{block}{Drifted bridge — advection--diffusion semigroups $\Qcal_\tau=e^{\tau\mathcal{L}}$, $\Qcal^{\dagger}_\tau=e^{\tau\mathcal{L}^\ast}$}
\[
    \underbrace{\partial_\tau\phi=\bt\cdot\grad\phi+\gamma\Delta\phi}_{\Qcal:\ \text{non-conservative, backward}},
    \qquad
    \underbrace{\partial_\tau\phi=-\dive(\bt\phi)+\gamma\Delta\phi}_{\Qcal^{\dagger}:\ \text{conservative, forward}} .
\]
\end{block}

## Structure

| section | frames | content |
|---|---|---|
| *(kept)* Recap | 4 | Fokker–Planck, heat & advection–diffusion semigroups $\mathcal{Q}/\mathcal{Q}^\dagger$, CDI, transport maps $T,S$ |
| *(kept)* Drifts | 6 | oblique θ-β-M, FFD registration → β |
| **Self-Conditioned Drift** | 3 | the bootstrap $\beta^{(k+1)}=b^{(k)}$, exact β(t) + the Q/Q† direction trap, FFD seeding + endpoint clip |
| **Results — Mach** | 12 | survey design, 3-way snapshots + abs-error at M 1.3–1.4 / 2.0–2.1 / 2.9–3.0, density transport, drift field, per-band gain heatmaps |
| **Results — AoA** | 5 | snapshots + abs-error at 0→1° and 3→4°, AoA-axis heatmap |
| **Error Analysis** | 15 | err vs Mach (AoA 0 and 2), crossover table, err vs AoA, drift-ranking table, then γ / t / h / SB-vs-FFD / heatmap / aero / transport / cost / IPFP, summary |

Snapshot frames are 3-up (BaryCDI | FFD | Linear) at $t=0.5$ so the comparison is on one slide. Text is minimal — the two tables (Mach crossover, drift ranking) carry the numbers, everything else is a figure.

**I dropped 24 frames** from the old deck: the 12 per-γ absolute-error slides for oblique and FFD, the 4 FFD-registration-as-interpolator slides, and the 7 old single-pair sweep frames. All were the 2.00→2.50 pair only, now superseded by the 22-band survey — and that pair is the *0.5-wide* one, so its numbers aren't comparable to the survey bands anyway. Your original is at `/tmp/SB_sweep_backup.tex` and in git if you want any back.

One preamble change: added `\usepackage{array}`, needed for the `>{\bfseries}` column in the results tables.

Two things you may want to adjust. I used `drift_SBsquared_exact+ffd` for the Mach snapshots and `drift_ffd` for the AoA ones (SB² is available on both, but it's the weak drift on the AoA axis) — say the word if you'd rather show `oblique` throughout, since that's the drift that actually wins. And I picked three representative Mach bands out of 22; the per-band figures all exist, so adding more is one `figframe` line each.

def plot_gain_heatmap(rows, hmode, outdir):
    gammas = sorted({r["gamma"] for r in rows})
    M = np.full((len(DRIFT_ORDER), len(gammas)), np.nan)
    for i, drift in enumerate(DRIFT_ORDER):
        for r in _by_drift(rows, drift):
            j = gammas.index(r["gamma"])
            if np.isfinite(r["BaryCDI_l2_mean"]) and np.isfinite(r["Linear_l2_mean"]):
                M[i, j] = r["BaryCDI_l2_mean"] / r["Linear_l2_mean"]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(1.1 * len(gammas) + 2, 3.2))
    im = ax.imshow(M, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=0.0, vmax=2.0, aspect="auto")
    ax.set_xticks(range(len(gammas)), [f"{g:g}" for g in gammas], rotation=45)
    ax.set_yticks(range(len(DRIFT_ORDER)), DRIFT_ORDER)
    ax.set_xlabel(r"$\gamma_{\min}$")
    for i in range(M.shape[0]):
        for j in range(M.shape[1]):
            if np.isfinite(M[i, j]):
                ax.text(j, i, f"{M[i, j]:.2f}", ha="center", va="center",
                        fontsize=8,
                        color="white" if abs(M[i, j] - 1) > 0.6 else "black")
    fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label="mean-t L2  BaryCDI / Linear   (<1 beats linear)")
    ax.set_title(f"SB gain over linear — hessian_mode = {hmode}")
    fig.tight_layout()
    f = os.path.join(outdir, f"gain_heatmap_{hmode}.png")
    fig.savefig(f, dpi=200, bbox_inches="tight");  plt.close(fig)
    print(f"  wrote {f}")


def plot_diagnostics(rows, hmode, outdir):
```

## Claude  ·  2026-08-31T12:21:06.800Z

The regeneration is still running in the background. Here's where things stand.

## What I changed in the heatmaps

**Empty rows are gone.** Per-band figures were showing three blank white strips for the `SBsquared` variants that were never run on that band — they carried no information while squeezing the rows that did.

**The scale no longer saturates.** `vmin=0, vmax=2` was hard-clipping everything above 2, so 3.24 / 3.29 / 3.32 all rendered as the same dark red — the ordering was invisible exactly where the spread is widest. Now a `TwoSlopeNorm` pinned at **1.0** (parity with Linear) with limits from the data, so blue still means "beats Linear" but the real range shows.

**Title and colorbar no longer collide.** The title now wraps to a second line, and the label — previously truncated mid-word to `"<1 beats Li…"` — reads in full.

**Cell labels pick their colour from the cell's own luminance** instead of a fixed distance from 1.0, which had left dark-red cells with unreadable text.

## The part worth a second look

Dropping empty rows wasn't sufficient — a solid 4×6 white block remained, because the `SBsquared*` drifts were never run at the six tightest γ rungs (1e-6…5e-5) that only `null`/`oblique`/`ffd` covered. Deleting those columns would have satisfied "no white cells" while discarding a genuinely important result, so instead the function now **groups columns by which drifts they cover and emits one fully-populated heatmap per group**. No white cells, nothing thrown away.

That second block is worth putting on a slide by itself, which I did:

| γ | 1e-6 | 2e-6 | 5e-6 | 1e-5 | 2e-5 | 5e-5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| null | **1.72** | 1.71 | 1.63 | 1.31 | 0.84 | 0.64 |
| oblique | 0.41 | 0.41 | 0.40 | 0.40 | 0.38 | 0.37 |
| ffd | 0.39 | 0.39 | 0.39 | 0.38 | 0.38 | 0.38 |

Below γ=1e-5 the driftless kernel collapses past Linear while both drifted kernels hold a floor at 0.37–0.41. That's the clearest single view of what β actually buys — stability, not accuracy — and it was previously hidden inside the white block.

Once the background job finishes, recompile with `cd SB && pdflatex SB_sweep.tex` (twice). The deck is now 48 frames; all the per-band heatmaps it references will have been rewritten in place, and I've added the extended-γ frame after the main heatmap. I'll confirm the figure count when the run reports back.

## Claude  ·  2026-08-31T12:24:52.769Z

Done — deck recompiles to **48 pages**, all 42 figure references resolve, no errors.

## Heatmap fixes

**No white cells anywhere.** Two separate causes, fixed differently:

- *Empty rows* — per-band figures had three blank strips for `SBsquared` variants never run on that band. Dropped.
- *A 4×6 white block* in the aggregate figure, because the `SBsquared*` drifts don't exist at the six tightest γ rungs (1e-6…5e-5). Deleting those columns would have satisfied "no white" while discarding a real result, so the function now **groups columns by which drifts they cover and emits one fully-populated heatmap per group**. Nothing white, nothing lost.

**Missing information restored:**
- The scale was hard-clipped at `vmax=2`, painting 3.24 / 3.29 / 3.32 identical dark red — the ordering was invisible exactly where the spread is largest. Now `TwoSlopeNorm` pinned at 1.0 (parity with Linear) with limits from the data.
- The colorbar label was truncated mid-word (`"<1 beats Li…"`); the title ran into it. Title now wraps, label reads in full.
- Cell labels take their colour from the cell's own luminance instead of a fixed distance from 1.0, which had left dark-red cells unreadable.

62 heatmaps regenerated. Only one `_blk1` file exists, which is correct — only the legacy 2.00→2.50 pair has the extended γ ladder; every survey band is a uniform 3-γ grid and forms a single complete block.

That extended block was worth surfacing, so it's now its own slide (p. 43):

| γ | 1e-6 | 2e-6 | 5e-6 | 1e-5 | 2e-5 | 5e-5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| null | **1.72** | 1.71 | 1.63 | 1.31 | 0.84 | 0.64 |
| oblique | 0.41 | 0.41 | 0.40 | 0.40 | 0.38 | 0.37 |
| ffd | 0.39 | 0.39 | 0.39 | 0.38 | 0.38 | 0.38 |

Below γ=1e-5 the driftless kernel collapses past Linear while both drifted kernels hold at 0.37–0.41 — the clearest single view that β buys stability rather than accuracy, and it was previously buried inside the white block.

One thing I did not change: the main heatmap is still dense (7 drifts × 12 γ at ~0.5 cm per cell), so on a projector the annotations will be small. If that matters, the natural cut is dropping `SBsquared` and `SBsquared_exact` — the unseeded variants that the paired test showed are superseded by their `+ffd` counterparts — which would take it to 5 rows.

All four changes are in — deck compiles to **47 pages**, 42 figures, no errors.

**Deleted** frame 39 (Error vs. t) and frame 44 (Aerodynamic Coefficients).

**SB² is now two frames, exact only.** The frozen-at-*t*=0.5 variant is gone entirely — no mention of it. Frame 13 gives the drift in one equation with its full time dependence,

$$\beta^{(k+1)}(t) = \beta^{(k)}(t) + 2\gamma_k \nabla g^{(k)}_t$$

plus the two things a reader needs: it's a fixed point of the map, and Q reads β backward while Q† reads it forward. Frame 14 keeps the FFD seed and the endpoint clip.

**New figure** — `err_vs_mach_alldrifts_0.0001.png`, added at frames 34 and 35 (AoA 0 and 2). Every drift's BaryCDI curve plus Linear and FFD on a single log axis, x = band midpoint, so the 2.50→2.60 bridge sits at **M = 2.55** as you asked. Linear and FFD are drawn once each rather than repeated per panel, since neither depends on the drift.

It makes three things visible that the per-panel version could not:

- **FFD (red) is below every drift for M < 2.25** — the registration beats the bridge built on it across the whole low range.
- **Linear (black) crosses under everything at M ≈ 2.3** and stays lowest to M = 3.
- **`null` (blue) is the only unstable curve** — it spikes to 4e-3 at M = 2.75 while the other three sit near 6e-4. `oblique`, `ffd` and `SBsquared_exact+ffd` overlap almost everywhere, which is the drift-degeneracy result shown directly rather than inferred from a table.

The three drifted curves overlapping so tightly is worth knowing before you present: on this axis the 3–7% margin that the paired test found is not visually resolvable, so frame 38's table is what carries the drift ranking, not this plot.

## Claude  ·  2026-08-31T12:34:47.948Z

Definitive. At the spike bands the driftless IPFP **oscillates** rather than converging:

| band | last 5 residuals | min | final |
|---|---|---|---|
| M2.90–3.00 | 0.59, 1.42, 0.19, 0.23, **4.06** | 6.8e-2 | 4.06 |
| M2.80–2.90 | 0.68, 0.98, 2.20, 2.99, **1.09** | 6.8e-1 | 1.09 |
| M2.60–2.70 *(no spike)* | 3.3e-6, 3.5e-6, 3.5e-6, 3.4e-6, **3.2e-6** | 3.2e-6 | 3.2e-6 |

**The peaks are IPFP non-convergence, not a physical effect.** The residual jumps an order of magnitude between consecutive iterations and never settles, so the reported field is whatever iterate the loop happened to be on when it hit the 1000-iteration cap. That's why the spikes look random and alternate band to band (2.35 bad, 2.45 fine, 2.55 bad, 2.65 fine…) — it's essentially a coin flip per band.

The mechanism is the classic Sinkhorn failure at too-small ε. At γ=1e-4 the heat kernel has σ=√(2γ)≈0.014, about **0.6 cells**, while at high Mach the shock displacement between M and M+0.1 exceeds that. With a kernel narrower than the transport distance the scaling factors must be astronomical — `den_T_max` hits **1.8e+264** at M2.70–2.80 — and the log-domain updates overshoot. The drifted kernels don't have this problem because advection carries mass to the target, so the residual correction stays small: `ffd` converges on 9 bands with residuals ~1e-7, `null` on 2.

This is the same "β buys stability, not accuracy" result as the extended-γ heatmap, now visible band by band.

## Claude  ·  2026-08-31T12:36:28.229Z

Those peaks are **numerical, not physical** — the driftless IPFP fails to converge on exactly those bands.

## Evidence

Comparing the residual trajectory at a spike band against a clean one:

| band | last 5 residuals | min | final | γ=1e-4 result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| M2.90–3.00 | 0.59, 1.42, 0.19, 0.23, **4.06** | 6.8e-2 | 4.06 | spike |
| M2.80–2.90 | 0.68, 0.98, 2.20, 2.99, **1.09** | 6.8e-1 | 1.09 | spike |
| M2.60–2.70 | 3.3e-6, 3.5e-6, 3.5e-6, 3.4e-6, **3.2e-6** | 3.2e-6 | 3.2e-6 | clean |

At the spike bands the residual jumps an order of magnitude *between consecutive iterations* and never settles. It isn't converging slowly — it's **oscillating**. So the reported field is whichever iterate happened to be current when the loop hit its 1000-iteration cap, which is why the spikes look random and alternate band to band (2.35 bad, 2.45 fine, 2.55 bad, 2.65 fine…). Each is effectively a coin flip.

## Why the driftless kernel specifically

Classic Sinkhorn failure at too-small ε. At γ=1e-4 the heat kernel has σ=√(2γ)≈0.014 — about **0.6 cells** at h=0.025 — while at high Mach the shock displacement across a 0.10 band exceeds that. With a kernel narrower than the transport distance the scaling factors have to be astronomical: `den_T_max` reaches **1.8e+264** at M2.70–2.80, spanning ~300 orders of magnitude against `den_T_min` ≈ 3e-36. The log-domain updates then overshoot and ring.

The drifted kernels avoid it because advection carries mass toward the target, so the residual correction stays small. Across the 22 bands: **`ffd` converges on 9 with residuals ~1e-7; `null` on 2.** Same "β buys stability, not accuracy" result as the extended-γ heatmap, now band by band.

## What I changed

The plot was presenting an artifact as data, so non-converged points are now ringed in crimson with a legend entry, and the slide carries a one-line explanation. Threshold is residual > 1e-3, which cleanly separates all five spikes (2.7e-3 … 4.06) from the worst converged run (2.4e-4) — I'd first set 1e-2, which missed the M2.35 spike. `ipfp_res` and `converged` are now also columns in `err_by_mach_interval.csv`. Deck recompiles at 47 pages.

Worth deciding before the talk: those five `null` points are not measurements of anything, so you may prefer to drop them rather than ring them. I've left them visible because the failure is itself the argument for using a drift — but if the slide is meant to compare drift *accuracy*, they're noise on the axis.

========== FRAME 3 ==========
\begin{frame}{Recap — Heat and Advection--Diffusion Semigroups}

Hopf--Cole ($\eta=e^{f}$, $\eta^\ast=e^{g}$) linearizes the optimality system into
two transport--diffusion PDEs, whose transition operators are the SB kernel.

\begin{block}{Driftless bridge ($\bt\equiv0$) — heat semigroup $\Pcal_\tau=e^{\tau\gamma\Delta}$}
\[
    \partial_\tau\phi=\gamma\,\Delta\phi,\qquad \partial_n\phi|_{\partial\Omega}=0
    \quad(\text{Neumann, no-flux}).
\]
\end{block}

\begin{block}{Drifted bridge — advection--diffusion semigroups $\Qcal_\tau=e^{\tau\mathcal{L}}$, $\Qcal^{\dagger}_\tau=e^{\tau\mathcal{L}^\ast}$}
\[
    \underbrace{\partial_\tau\phi=\bt\cdot\grad\phi+\gamma\Delta\phi}_{\Qcal:\ \text{non-conservative, backward}},
    \qquad
    \underbrace{\partial_\tau\phi=-\dive(\bt\phi)+\gamma\Delta\phi}_{\Qcal^{\dagger}:\ \text{conservative, forward}} .
\]
\end{block}

IPFP in log-potential form:
\[
    f^{(k+1)}=\log\mu-\log\Qcal_1\!\bigl[e^{g^{(k)}}\bigr],
    \qquad
    g^{(k+1)}=\log\nu-\log\Qcal^{\dagger}_1\!\bigl[e^{f^{(k+1)}}\bigr].
\]

$\bt\equiv0\Rightarrow\Qcal_1=\Qcal^{\dagger}_1=\Pcal_1$.

## Claude  ·  2026-08-31T12:55:51.435Z

**Frame 13 — the idea.**

Every drift so far came from outside the bridge. Here the bridge supplies its own: at each rung of the γ-ladder, take the drift from the previous rung's solution.

$$\beta^{(k+1)}(t) = \beta^{(k)}(t) + 2\gamma_k \nabla g^{(k)}_t$$

That right-hand side is just the SB optimal drift $b$ of stage $k$ — so you're saying "whatever bridge I just solved, use *its* velocity field as the reference for the next, tighter one." Stored as a $K\times N\times 2$ stack (β at K times, N cells, 2 components) and fed to the kernel at every substep.

Two claims on the slide:

- **Well posed.** If β is already optimal, the correction $\nabla g$ vanishes, so $\beta'=\beta$. The true SB solution is a fixed point of the map — the scheme can't drift away from the answer, which is what makes iterating it legitimate rather than a hack.
- **Time direction.** Q propagates the backward wave function (SB time $1-\tau$), Q† the forward one ($\tau$), so the two solvers must index the same β stack in *opposite* directions. Get it wrong and you still get a plausible-looking answer — which is why the slide quotes the adjoint check $\langle Qu,v\rangle=\langle u,Q^\dagger v\rangle$ holding to 7e-15 (an un-mirrored control fails by 183%).

**Frame 14 — making it actually work.** Two fixes, because the naive version loses.

- **Seed.** Starting from a heat bridge (β≡0) at γ=0.2 recovers a huge, void-dominated $2\gamma\nabla g$, and the whole mid-ladder is spent washing it out. So start from the FFD registration and hold it **fixed** until γ drops below γ\*=1e-3; only then self-condition. Above the switch it is literally a `drift_ffd` run — verified to 6 digits.
- **Endpoint clip.** $g_t=\log Q_{1-t}[e^g]$, and at $t=1$ the operator $Q_0$ is the identity, so β picks up the gradient of the *raw* log-potential. The table is the measurement: |2γ∇g| goes 1.35 → 1.79 → **13.76** from t=0 to t=1. Since $|\beta|_{\max}$ sets the advective CFL for every stage, that one slice would slow the entire ladder. Fix: sample $t\in[0.2,\,0.8]$ instead of $[0,1]$.

The frozen-at-$t$=0.5 variant never sees t=1, which is why exactness *alone* made things worse and needed the clip to be usable at all.

One note: the sweep-figure regeneration I started is still running in the background, so the heatmap titles won't show the new mesh/AoA labels until it finishes.

## Claude  ·  2026-08-31T12:58:58.067Z

**Page 38 — "Which Drift? — Paired per-Band Comparison"**

This is the slide that answers *which drift to use*, and it exists because the obvious way of answering it is wrong.

**Why not just average.** Take each drift's mean error over all its bands and compare. That fails here for two reasons: `oblique` has no solution below M≈1.25 so it's missing the 5 hardest bands, and the legacy pair is 0.5 Mach wide while the survey bands are 0.1. Both inflate or deflate a drift's mean for reasons that have nothing to do with the drift. Averaging that way made `oblique` look 29% better than `ffd`; the real figure is 5%.

**What the slide does instead.** Pair the drifts *band by band* — same Mach interval, same γ, same mesh — and ask how often one beats the other. That's the `wins` column (e.g. 33/39). The `median ratio` is the typical size of the gap, and `p` is an exact two-sided sign test: the probability of seeing that lopsided a win count if the two drifts were really equivalent.

**How to read the rows.**

| | |
|---|---|
| `oblique vs ffd`, 33/39, ratio 0.931, p<1e-4 | oblique is better on 33 of 39 bands, typically by 6.9%, and that's not chance |
| `ffd vs SB²+ffd` at γ=1e-3 | *identical* — because `BOOT_SWITCH`=1e-3 holds the FFD seed fixed above that γ, so no bootstrapping has happened yet. Not a result, a definition |

**The headline:** oblique wins at every γ rung, and its margin *grows* as γ falls — 3.1% → 5.3% → 6.9%. Consistent across ~35 independent bands.

**The two conclusion boxes.** Left: oblique is best, but only defined for M≳1.25, so it can't be your drift in the subsonic/detached bands at all. Right: SB²+ffd is essentially ffd — it gains 2.9% on the Mach axis but loses 93% on the AoA axis, in exchange for a whole extra IPFP anneal. That's the slide's practical verdict: the reconditioned bootstrap isn't worth its cost.

**One trick worth knowing if you're asked.** The validity check for this whole table is the `Linear` column in the regime tables: Linear can't depend on the drift, so if it ever differs between two drift rows, those rows aren't averaging the same bands and the comparison is void. That's exactly how the unequal-band-set problem was caught.

## Claude  ·  2026-08-31T16:02:05.022Z

Not a missing sweep — **missing command**. The bump runs completed (198/198 `metrics.json`, so your re-run after the `le_shock_geometry` fix worked), but `sweep_analysis.py` defaults to the *diamond* roots only:

```python
default=["outputs/Mach_interpolation/diamond/iso/hessian",
         "outputs/AoA_interpolation/diamond/iso/hessian"]
```

so it never looked at `.../bump/...`. I've now run both on bump:

```bash
uv run python SB/sweep_analysis.py   --root outputs/Mach_interpolation/bump/iso/hessian
uv run python SB/interval_analysis.py --root outputs/Mach_interpolation/bump/iso/hessian
```

`outputs/Mach_interpolation/bump/iso/hessian/_sweep/` now exists with the full figure set plus `sweep_summary.csv`, `err_by_mach_interval.csv` and `regime_summary.csv`.

**First look at the bump numbers** (matched bands, γ=1e-4, 18 attached bands):

| regime | BaryCDI | Linear | FFD |
|---|---|---|---|
| attached | 5.16–5.37e-3 | 6.77e-3 | **3.17e-3** |
| detached | 2.48–2.76e-2 | 3.47e-2 | **1.97e-2** |
| subsonic | 2.72–3.10e-2 | 3.30e-2 | **2.13e-2** |

Three things carry over from the diamond, which is worth knowing before you read further into it:

- **FFD still wins everywhere** — 3.17e-3 vs BaryCDI's ~5.2e-3 in the attached regime, a 63% gap, wider than the diamond's ~39%.
- **The drifts are degenerate again** — null / ffd / SB²+ffd land within 4% of each other (5.16 / 5.36 / 5.37e-3). And on the bump `null` is nominally *best*, which is the strongest form of the "β buys stability, not accuracy" result so far.
- **Errors are ~3× the diamond's** at matched bands (5.2e-3 vs 1.7e-3). Not obviously meaningful — the two cases have different geometries, cell counts (14 178 vs 20 190) and marginal normalisation, so cross-case magnitudes aren't directly comparable.

Two caveats on the bump results specifically. The angle and Rankine–Hugoniot metrics are **NaN by construction** there — I made them skip for non-wedge geometry, since θ-β-M has no meaning without a leading-edge wedge — so `transport_*.png` has two empty panels for bump. And no `err_vs_h` (single mesh) and no AoA axis, both expected.

The diamond regeneration I started earlier is still running in the background; I'll report when it lands.

## Claude  ·  2026-09-01T12:33:37.469Z

`.gitignore` is updated (the cause: `outputs/` was never in it). Here's the recipe.

## Commit code only — what you asked

```bash
cd ~/GenerativePDE
git add .gitignore CLAUDE.md SB/ run_*.sbatch
git commit -m "Mach/AoA interval survey: case-aware grids, interval analysis, deck"
```

`git add SB/` is safe now — the LaTeX aux/log files are ignored, and `outputs/` isn't under it. Check with `git status` before committing; nothing under `outputs/` should be staged.

**Don't use `git add -A` or `git add .`** — that would pull in 1356 `metrics.json` (**177 MB**) from the new untracked directories, since I deliberately left JSON un-ignored.

## Stop the 5072 heavy files already tracked

`.gitignore` has no effect on files git already tracks — 5025 PNGs and 47 npz/npy (299 MB) are in your index and will keep coming back:

```bash
git ls-files -z 'outputs/*.png' 'outputs/*.npz' 'outputs/*.npy' | xargs -0 git rm --cached --quiet
git commit -m "Untrack generated figures and field dumps"
```

`--cached` removes them from the index only — **every file stays on disk**. Your working tree is untouched.

## Two things worth deciding

**`metrics.json` — 1356 files, 177 MB.** I left these trackable on purpose: they're the raw per-run record and the *only* artefact here that can't be regenerated without re-running the GPU jobs. The PNGs and npz all come back from `SB/main.py`. If 177 MB is too much, the `_sweep/*.csv` files (12 files, a few hundred KB) hold the aggregated numbers — add `outputs/**/metrics.json` to `.gitignore` and track only those. That trades the ability to re-aggregate differently later.

**Your `.git` is already 2.5 GB** and untracking won't shrink it — history still contains every blob ever committed. Only a history rewrite (`git-filter-repo --path outputs --invert-paths`) reclaims that, and it rewrites every commit hash. Worth it only if the repo size is actually blocking you; I'd leave it alone unless you need to push somewhere with a size cap.

One aside: `SB/SB_sweep.pdf` shows as deleted because the compiled PDF got renamed to `SB_sweep0.pdf` (identical 10 713 897 bytes). Either rename it back before committing or `git rm --cached SB/SB_sweep.pdf` — a 10 MB binary that `pdflatex` regenerates probably shouldn't be tracked at all.
